items.title: The Maya used so much red paint that they poisoned their water with mercury, mud sediments reveal
items.snippet: Researchers found extreme levels of mercury in sediment cores in Mexico ‪—‬ and it’s all because the Maya loved red paint.

items.title: Why the tropics lose the most birds when cities expand
items.snippet: Tropical ecosystems are famous for their teeming, exuberant diversity. In fact, the dramatic increase in biodiversity from the poles to the tropics—known as the latitudinal diversity gradient—is pervasive across branches of the tree of life, and fossil evidence suggests it has existed for millennia.

items.snippet: Private retirement savings are an increasingly important topic in public debate. items.title: Student finds proof of rare wild cat in northern New Mexico
items.snippet: Armed with dozens of motion-sensing cameras, William Grooms spent this past summer documenting wildlife across Carson National Forest in northern New Mexico. It was his first field season collecting photos for a two-year study to understand how forest structure influences biodiversity in the Southern Rocky Mountains.

items.title: The hidden ways insects support animal life—from habitat to health—go way beyond being food
items.snippet: There are at least 14 million insect species on Earth, and they play highly diverse roles in sustaining the natural world. Insects provide many well-known benefits—what scientists often call "ecosystem services." For example, you can thank a bee or a hoverfly for pollinating wildflowers and agricultural crops, or credit dung beetles for decomposing manure and other waste materials.

items.title: Different text genres help doctoral students adapt their writing to reach new readers
items.snippet: An academic abstract, a blog post and a public outreach article all place different demands on the writer. Readers' prior knowledge varies, as does the purpose of the text and what needs explaining. Mastering one kind of text therefore does not automatically mean being able to write another.

items.title: Two paths, one flux: Trapped ions simulate Aharonov–Bohm interference in a lattice gauge theory
items.snippet: In a new Nature Physics study, researchers demonstrated the Aharonov-Bohm effect in a quantum simulation of a lattice gauge theory using a hybrid trapped-ion quantum computer.
